approved: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2017

Labor supported the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2017, which brings digital currency exchanges under the regime, but criticised the government for a light-touch approach including a $10,000 reporting threshold that misses 99% of cash transactions, and for cutting AUSTRAC's budget by $7 million in 2014-15 and $19 million in 2016-17.

The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2017 was criticised as weak and insufficient, estimated to address only about five per cent of necessary reforms while leaving major gaps in coverage for real estate agents, lawyers, and accountants. Citing Australia's failure in all 10 Transparency International priority areas, placement on the FATF watchlist, the Commonwealth Bank's ~54,000 breaches, and $31.9 billion in 2015-16 Chinese residential investment, the argument highlighted unchecked money-laundering risks in Australian real estate.

The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2017 implements the first phase of reforms from a statutory review, but Labor supports it while arguing it may not go far enough given recent scandals like the Commonwealth Bank’s noncompliance. The speaker criticised the government for cutting AUSTRAC’s budget by $7 million in 2014-15 and $19 million in 2016-17, despite international pressure to strengthen enforcement.

The speaker supported the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2017 as a first-phase reform but argued it falls short of addressing all gaps, including non-financial sectors and cryptocurrencies, while criticising the government for cutting $7 million from AUSTRAC in 2014‑15 and $19 million in 2016‑17, and for the Commonwealth Bank’s alleged failure to report $624.7 million in cash transactions.

The bill updates Australia’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing regime to regulate digital currencies, deregulates cash-in-transit operators (saving $326 million over 10 years) and some insurance intermediaries (saving over $500,000), and enhances search and seizure powers while strengthening AUSTRAC’s supervisory and enforcement role.

The speaker argued the government's amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Bill 2017 on stored value cards only "tinker at the edges" and will not significantly impact money laundering or terrorism financing, despite noting AUSTRAC's risk assessment warning these cards are increasingly used by criminals and terrorists, including in the 2015 Paris attacks.
